title: Smarter Quote Submissions: Configurable Email Attachments in SAP Sales Cloud V2
author: ashwin_shetty2
text:
SAP Sales CloudV2 now gives sales administrators separate control over what gets attached to quote emails , depending on whether the email is triggered by the Submit action or created manually by a sales rep. And with a bit of integration work, this opens a powerful door: automatically sending S/4HANA generated quote PDFs to customers, without the sales rep ever touching the backend system 
 Quote Submission 
 There are two separate workflows to submit a Sales Quote. The Submit action and a manually created email from a quote are treated as distinct events, each with its own attachment configuration. 

 Trigger Configured In Options 
 Submit action Document Types → Email Attachment None / Generated Quote PDF / Quote Email Attachment 
 Manual email from quote General →Defaults Email Attachment None / Generated Quote PDF / Quote Email Attachment 
 This separation matters because the intent behind each action is different. A submission is a formal, often automated step where you want consistency enforced. A manually created email might be a follow-up, a revision note, or a relationship touchpoint , where the default might differ by business context. 
 Submit Sales Quote PDF from S/4 Hana 
 In many organisations, the main quote PDF lives in S/4HANA, it carries pricing, legal terms, and output determined by S/4 output management. Sales reps working in Sales Cloud shouldn't have to switch systems just to retrieve and attach that PDF. They dont have to if you follow the below steps 
 1 . Upload the S/4 PDF via the Document Service API 
 exposes adocument-service API that allows external systems to upload documents directly into the tenant. Using a custom enhancement or integration (e.g. triggered when the S/4 quote is released or output is generated), the S/4 PDF can be pushed into the Sales Cloud tenant automatically. 
 You can also refer to this blog for details on how to work with document -service API https://community.sap.com/t5/crm-and-cx-blog-posts-by-sap/how-to-use-document-service-api-to-upload-documents-into-sales-amp-service/ba-p/13719891 
 Make sure the document is linked to the corresponding sales quote using the attachment type "Email Attachment" . This is the key this attachment type is what the new Email Attachment configuration recognises and acts on. 
 2. c onfigure the Document Type 
 In the Document Types settings, set the Email Attachment dropdown to Quote Email Attachment for the relevant document type. Ensure Email on Submit is enabled. 
 3 . Submit 
 When the sales rep hits Submit, the system picks up the linked "Email Attachment" type document attached to the sales quote , which is the S/4-generated PDF, and includes it in the outbound email. 
 Configuration Summary 
 Document Types (for Submit behaviour): 
 User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Sales Quotes → Document Types 
 Enable Email on Submit 
 Set Email Attachment to Quote Email Attachment 
 General (for manually created emails): 
 User Menu → System Settings → All Settings → Sales Quotes → General 
 Under Default Email Attachment, select Quote Email Attachment (or whichever default fits your process) 
 Integration side: 
 On S/4 quote release or output generation, call the document-service API in Sales & Service Cloud v2 to upload the PDF 
 Link the uploaded document to the sales quote with attachment type Email Attachment 

 What looks like a simple configuration addition delivers two meaningful improvements. First, administrators can now separately define what gets attached when a quote is submitted versus when a sales rep manually sends an email from a quote giving precise control over two distinct customer touchpoints. Second, the "Quote Email Attachment" type opens the door to richer integration scenarios

title: SAP Continuous Influence for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition: Feedback Session Overview
author: DoreenBaseler
text:
SAP Continuous Influence provides customers and partners with a direct channel to share product improvement requests and influence the future direction of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. This article provides a comprehensive overview of all currently available SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition feedback sessions, helping you quickly identify the correct session for submitting requests or voting on existing requests. 
 What Is a Feedback Session? 
 A feedback session is a product area or topic-specific campaign within SAP Continuous Influence where customers can: 
 Submit improvement requests 
 Vote on existing requests 
 Collaborate with the SAP product team on future innovations 
 Please note that not every product topic has a dedicated feedback session. 
 SAP reserves the right to open, extend, consolidate, scale down, or close feedback sessions at any time. 
 Voting thresholds and processing times apply to all sessions and may vary slightly between standard sessions and dedicated Integration and Extensibility sessions. 
 Before You Submit a Request 
 To ensure efficient processing and avoid duplicate requests, please follow these steps: 
 Search for an existing request related to your topic. 
 If a similar request already exists, support it by voting. 
 If no similar request exists, submit a new request in the appropriate feedback session. 
 Standard Session (Multiple-Vote Principle) 

 Requests in standard sessions are prioritized through community voting and are typically reviewed in greater detail only after the required voting threshold has been achieved: 
 SAP Central Business Configuration for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and Private Edition, Advanced Variant Configuration SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and Private Edition, Environment, Health, and Safety Management 
 SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and Private Edition, Group Reporting

 Integration and Extensibility Sessions ( One-Vote Principle) 
 In Integration and Extensibility sessions, every submitted enhancement request is individually assessed by SAP and receives a qualified response, independent of voting results:

 Alternatively, you can access SAP Continuous Influence by signing in to your SAP for Me account and navigating to Portfolio & Products → Customer Influence . 
 Get Involved 
 Your feedback helps shape future innovations in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Whether you submit a new idea or vote for an existing enhancement request, your participation directly contributes to product evolution and prioritization. 
 Visit the relevant session, review existing requests, and make your voice heard through SAP Continuous Influence.

title: EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD BAdI Implementation for RESTRICT_CANCEL
author: marcel_schaefer
text:
The following blog post is relevant only for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. Please note that Developer Extensibility is required. 

 Use case: 
 You are trying to cancel a Billing Document in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud, but the system prevents it with the error message "Document XXXXXXXX: Unable to cancel document; Cancel related eDocument first". Alternative Use Case could be, that the cancellation of a billing document is allowed, but you want to further restrict it. 

 Important Warning: 
 This BAdI should only be used for special case handling allowing the cancellation or if you want to further restrict the cancellation. Please understand the country process in detail before overwriting standard country logic with the BAdI. If for example an eDocument is submitted and accepted by the authority, an invoice cancellations is often not allowed - the correction then has to be done with an additional document like credit memo or an additional invoice. Please keep also in mind that using this BAdI method can lead to inconsistent business data in your system - e.g. accepted eDocument with cancelled invoice. In many country implementations it is allowed to cancel the billing document, when the eDocument is in cancelled state or you were able to delete the eDocument. 

 Implementation: 
 To implement the above requirement method "if_edoc_adaptor_cloud~restrict_cancel" in BAdI EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD (enhancement spot ES_EDOCUMENT_CLOUD). The method “restrict_cancel” receives the edocument data in the importing parameter “is_edocument” and source key and source type. The changing parameter “cv_restrict” allows you to control whether the electronic document can be cancelled or not - the value which is handed over is the determined value by standard. 
 Implementation Steps: 
 Create implementation for enhancement spot ES_DOCUMENT_CLOUD. 
 Create BAdI implementation for EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD. 
 (Optional) Create BAdI Filter for Country and/or Generic Filter. 
 Create implementing class for BAdI EDOC_ADAPTOR_CLOUD, which implements the interfaces "if_badi_interfaces" and "if_edoc_adaptor_cloud". 
 Implement method "is_relevant" of interface "if_edoc_adaptor_cloud" in your BAdI class. 
 Activate your BAdI implementation. METHOD if_edoc_adaptor_cloud~restrict_cancel.
 IF <your condition>.
 cv_restrict = abap_true/abap_false.
 ENDIF.
 ENDMETHOD.

title: A Practical Guide to Manage Tenant Connections in SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model
author: KarenSamantha_Robles
text:
As SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model landscapes grow, organizations typically operate across multiple tenants such as Development (DEV), Quality Assurance (QAS), and Production (PRD). While transporting environments between tenants is a standard practice, managing HANA Schema Connections across these environments can become a maintenance challenge. 
 A common question is: 
 How can you transport models across tenants without reconfiguring HANA Schema Connections after every transport? 
 The solution is Manage Tenant Connections , this feature allows you to create and maintain HANA Schema connection that is tenant-specific. By defining tenant-specific mappings, you can transport models between tenants without repeatedly updating connection settings. Each PaPM Cloud tenant can then independently control which physical HANA schema the connection points to. 

 Why Use Manage Tenant Connections? 
 By using tenant-specific connections, you can: 
 Keep the same HANA Schema Connection name across multiple tenants. 
 Reduce maintenance after transports. 
 Configure schema assignments independently per tenant. 
 Minimize the risk of errors caused by manual connection updates after transports. 
 Prepare your landscape for future changes without modifying existing models. 
 Bottom line: Consistent models, flexible schema assignments, and fewer deployment risks. 

 How It Works? 
 Imagine you have developed a model that uses the HANA Schema Connection CONSALES to read from or write to the SALES table. 
 By setting the connection's Tenant Specific property to Yes , each tenant can maintain its own schema assignment through Manage Tenant Connections . 

 In the Source Tenant, CONSALES points to FIN_SRC HANA Schema, while in the Target Tenant , CONSALES points to FIN_TGT HANA Schema. When the model is transported, nothing in the model needs to change. The same connection, table reference, and business logic are reused, while PAPM automatically resolves the correct schema based on the tenant-specific configuration. 

 How to Use Manage Tenant Connections? 
 Now that we've covered the concept and benefits of Manage Tenant Connections , let's walk through a practical example. 
 Disclaimer: The screenshots and configuration values shown in this guide are for illustration purposes only. Connection names, schema names, descriptions, and other values are sample data intended to demonstrate the setup process and may differ from your actual system landscape. 

 Prerequisite: 
 Before proceeding, ensure the following requirements are met: 
 You must have an access to Administration, Connection Management and Manage Tenant Connections. Refer to Role Templates in Universal Model 
 SAP Cloud Universal Model have the access to read or write in the HANA Schema. Refer to Database Administration in BYOD SAP HANA Cloud and Database Administration in BYOD SAP Datasphere 
 The HANA Schema Connection must be configured with Tenant Specific = Yes. Refer to Manage Connections: HANA Schema 
 The HANA Schema Connection Name must be identical across all tenants 

 Source Tenant Configuration 
 Step 1: Ensure Tenant-Specific Is Enabled for the HANA Schema Connection 
 Before configuring Manage Tenant Connections, verify that the HANA Schema Connection is configured with Tenant Specific = Yes . This setting allows each tenant to maintain its own schema mapping while using the same connection name across the landscape. 
 When reviewing the HANA Schema Connection: 
 a. Navigate to Manage Environment > Environment > Connections 
 b. Open the HANA Schema Connection that will be used by the model. 
 c. Verify that Tenant Specific is set to Yes . 
 Important: The connection name must remain identical across all tenants. When Tenant Specific is enabled, the schema assignment is maintained separately through Manage Tenant Connections, allowing the same model to be transported without modifying connection references. 

 Step 2: Configure Manage Tenant Connections 
 a. Navigate to Administration > Manage Tenant Connections 
 b. Select Create. 
 c. The Environment field is optional. Note that only activated environments will be displayed in the value help. Select HANA Schema as the Connection Target Type, then click Continue. 

 e. Enter the required values 

 Attribute 
 Value 

 Connection 
 Provide the HANA Schema Connection 

 Description 
 Optional 

 Target HANA Schema 
 Provide the Target HANA Schema for the Source Tenant 
 After saving, the CONSALES connection is mapped to the FIN_SRC schema. 

 Step 3: Export the Environment 
 Export the environment from the source tenant using the standard SAP PaPM Cloud export process. For detailed guidance, refer to the SAP Help documentation: Export Environment 

 Target Tenant Configuration 
 Step 1: Import the Environment to the target tenant 
 Import the environment to the target tenant using the standard SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model Import process. For detailed guidance, refer to the SAP Help documentation: Import Environment . At this stage, the environment can remain inactive. 

 Step 2: Configure Manage Tenant Connections in the target tenant 
 Before activating the imported environment, create the corresponding tenant connection in the target tenant. 
 Navigate to Administration > Manage Tenant Connections. 
 Select Create. 
 The Environment field is optional. Note that only activated environments will be displayed in the value help. Select HANA Schema as the Connection Target Type, then click Continue. 
 Use the same connection name used in the source tenant and specify the target schema. 

 Attribute 
 Value 

 Connection 
 Provide the HANA Schema Connection 

 Description 
 Optional 

 Target HANA Schema 
 Provide the Target HANA Schema for the Target Tenant 
 This is the key benefit of tenant-specific connections wherein the model remains identical while each tenant controls its own schema assignment. 

 IMPORTANT NOTE: 
 The Target HANA Schema maintained in the HANA Schema Connection serves as the connection definition; however, when Tenant Specific = Yes is enabled, the actual runtime schema for each tenant is controlled by Manage Tenant Connections. Therefore, always check Administration > Manage Tenant Connections to confirm the effective schema assignment. 

 Step 3: Activate The Environment and Perform Validation 
 After configuring the tenant connection: 
 Activate the imported environment. 
 Execute a process that uses the HANA Schema Connection (for example, a Reader or Writer function). 
 Verify that the operation uses the expected target schema. 

 Test Result: 
 In this example, a Writer function was executed after activation. 
 Although the model continued to reference the CONSALES connection, the target tenant's Manage Tenant Connections configuration redirected the operation to FIN_TGT. As expected, the data was successfully written to FIN_TGT.SALES without requiring any modifications to the transported model. 
 FIN_SRC.SALES 

 FIN_TGT.SALES 

 Final Thoughts: 
 Manage Tenant Connections is a simple yet powerful feature that helps organizations streamline their SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model. If you're working with a multi-tenant SAP PaPM Cloud landscape, implementing tenant-specific connections can save time, reduce manual effort, and make your deployments more reliable.

 Introduction 
 This is the fifth post in the series. In the previous post , we set up the Google OAuth client, created the External Authentication in Control Tower, registered it on the Desktop Agent, and built a small automation that searches Gmail and saves attachments to a local folder. That post ended with one search, one read, and a folder of PDFs. 
 Gmail offers a lot more than that. In this post we go through every Gmail activity BPA provides, one at a time, inside a single task automation. Along the way we make sure an email is never read twice, send a fresh email with attachments, reply to a thread, and finally delete an email. 
 Here's what we'll cover: 
 Searching Gmail and reading an email, with its attachments saved to a local folder 
 Moving a processed email from Inbox to a "read" label, so it's never fetched again 
 Sending an email with attachments 
 Replying and replying to all on an existing thread 
 Deleting an email (and why that one deserves extra care) 
 Cleaning up with Disconnect (Google) 
 The Gmail Activities at a Glance 
 With the Google Workspace SDK added to the project, searching for "Gmail" in the automation's Tools panel lists seven activities: Send Email, Search Emails, Read Email, Modify Email Labels, Send Reply, Reply All and Delete Email. It also lists the supporting data types, such as Gmail Attachments, Gmail Message Detail, Gmail Message Identifier, Gmail Parameters and Gmail Reply Parameters. Every activity we use in this post is highlighted below in red. 

 The finished automation with each Gmail activity highlighted, next to the Gmail activities in the Tools panel. 
 The flow reads top to bottom, and each group of steps maps to one part of this post: 
 Steps 3 to 6: search the inbox, check that something was found, empty the target folder, and read the email with its attachments. 
 Step 7: modify the labels on the email we just read. 
 Step 8: send a new email with attachments. 
 Steps 10 to 12: search for a thread, then reply to all and reply to it. 
 Steps 13 and 14: search for a temporary email and delete it. 
 Step 15: disconnect from Google. 
 Everything from step 1 (Select Google Authentication) sits inside the same Try / Catch pattern from the previous post, catching GmailError. 
 Before You Start 
 The External Authentication from the previous post needs the Gmail scope. That scope covers reading, sending and permanently deleting email, so nothing extra is needed for this post. If you ever add a scope, update the External Authentication in Control Tower and register it on the Desktop Agent again. 
 Create a Gmail label named BPA-Read manually in Gmail. The automation applies this label but does not create it. 
 Prepare three test emails with distinct subjects, so each part of the flow only touches its own email: Gmail-BPA (with three PDF attachments) for read and label, BPA-Gmail (a thread with a few participants) for the reply steps, and BPA-Delete for the delete step. 
 Use a test mailbox. The delete step is permanent. 
 Part 1: Search and Read an Email 
 This part repeats the idea from the previous post, so I'll keep it brief. The test email sits in the Inbox, with the subject Gmail-BPA and three invoice PDFs attached. 

 The test email in the Inbox, with three PDF attachments. 
 Search Emails (Gmail). I renamed this step "Search Emails (Gmail) for Read & Get Attachments" so it's easy to tell apart from the other searches later in the flow. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("Gmail-BPA"), so only emails still in the Inbox with that subject are returned. includeSpamTrash is false, and the output, messageIdentifiers, is the list of matches. 

 Search Emails (Gmail) for Read & Get Attachments. 
 Email Found? A Condition step checks Step3.messageIdentifiers.length > 0. If nothing matches, the default branch just logs a message. 

 The Email Found? condition. 
 Delete All Files. Before downloading, this empties the local target folder, so files from an earlier run are never picked up again. 

 Delete All Files on the target folder. 
 Read Email (Gmail). messageId is messageIdentifiers[0].messageId, location is fileSystem, and pathOrDriveId is the same target folder. The three PDFs are saved there, and the output messageDetail holds the email details. 

 Read Email (Gmail) saving the three attachments into the target folder. 
 Part 2: Modify Email Labels 
 Here is a problem with the flow so far: the email stays in the Inbox after we read it, so the next run would find and read it again. We solve that with Modify Email Labels (Gmail) , which moves the email out of the Inbox and into our BPA-Read label. Because the search query includes Label: Inbox, an email that has been moved never matches again. 
 Modify Email Labels (Gmail). messageId is messageIdentifiers[0].messageId, the same email we just read. labelsToAdd is a list holding BPA-Read, and labelsToRemove is a list holding Inbox. Both lists are entered as custom data, one string per label. 

 Modify Email Labels (Gmail) adding BPA-Read and removing Inbox. 
 Back in Gmail, the same email now carries the BPA-Read label instead of Inbox. 

 The processed email, now labelled BPA-Read. 
 This is the label approach I chose over the markAsRead option on Read Email. The email keeps its read or unread state, and the label gives you a visible record of what the automation has handled, which you can also search on in Gmail. 
 Part 3: Send Email 
 Next we send a new email using Send Email (Gmail) . All its inputs live in one custom data object called gmailParameters. 
 Fill in the recipient fields: to , plus optional cc and bcc (semicolon separated). I sent it to my own address for the test. 
 Set the subject ([BPA Auto] Invoice Attachments | Send Mail) and the body . isHtmlBody is false here, so the body is plain text. Set it to true if you want to send HTML. 

 Send Email (Gmail) --- recipients, subject, body and the start of the attachments list. 
 Add attachments . Each attachment is its own entry with attachFrom (fileSystem here) and a filePath. I attached the same three PDFs we downloaded in Part 1, purely for convenience. Any file path works, so you can attach whatever your scenario needs. 

 One attachment entry per file, each with attachFrom and filePath. 
 The email arrives with all three PDFs attached. 

 The email sent by the automation, with its three attachments. 
 Part 4: Reply and Reply All 
 To reply to an existing conversation, the automation needs to know which thread to reply into. For this I set up a separate test thread with a few participants, subject BPA-Gmail, and added a dedicated search step for it. 
 Search Emails (Gmail) To Reply. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("BPA-Gmail"), and the output is again messageIdentifiers, this time from step 10. 

 Search Emails (Gmail) To Reply. 
 Reply All (Gmail). The input is replyParamters (the spelling as it appears in the activity). threadId is messageIdentifiers[0].threadId from step 10, which is what places the reply inside the existing conversation. messageId, to, cc and bcc are left empty, and the body is the text to send. includeOriginalAttachments is false, and attachments can be added the same way as in Send Email. 

 Reply All (Gmail), with threadId taken from the search step. 
 Send Reply (Gmail). It has the same parameters as Reply All. The difference is in who receives the message: Reply All goes to everyone on the thread, while Send Reply goes back to a single recipient. 

 Send Reply (Gmail), with the same parameter structure. 
 In Gmail, both messages show up inside the original thread. In my test, the Reply All message went to all four other participants, and the Reply went to one. 

 The test thread, with the Reply All and Reply messages sent by the automation at the bottom. 
 Part 5: Delete Email 
 The last activity is Delete Email (Gmail) . As with replying, we first find the email, this time using a dedicated search step with the subject BPA-Delete. 
 Search Emails (Gmail) To Delete. The query is Label: Inbox subject:("BPA-Delete"), and the output messageIdentifiers comes from step 13. 

 Search Emails (Gmail) To Delete. 
 Delete Email (Gmail). The only required input is messageId, here messageIdentifiers[0].messageId from step 13. 

 Delete Email (Gmail) with the messageId from the search step. 
 This is the temporary email the automation removes: 

 The temporary email, before the automation runs. 
 This deletion is permanent. When you delete an email in the Gmail interface, it moves to Trash and is removed later, either after Gmail's retention period or when you empty the Trash yourself. The Delete Email activity does not do that. In my test the email was gone immediately and did not appear in Trash, which matches how Google describes the underlying delete call in the Gmail API: immediate and permanent, with no way to undo it. Treat this activity like a delete statement without a rollback. 
 Finishing Up: Disconnect (Google) 
 The last step of the flow, step 15, is Disconnect (Google) , which closes the connection to Google once the work is done. It sits after the Try / Catch block, so it runs on both the success and error paths. 
 Things to Keep in Mind 
 Be careful with delete. Use a precise query (here, a keyword unique to the temporary email), run it against a test mailbox first, and consider whether a label like BPA-Delete or a separate review step is safer for production scenarios. 
 Guard the later steps. In this flow, steps 10 to 14 sit outside the Email Found? condition, and they read messageIdentifiers[0]. If a search returns no results, that step has nothing to read. Wrapping each search-then-act pair in its own condition, like we did for step 4, avoids that. 
 First match only. Using index 0 means each run handles one email per search. For several emails, loop over messageIdentifiers. 
 Labels must exist. Modify Email Labels uses the label names you enter, so create BPA-Read in Gmail first and keep the spelling identical. 
 Gmail search syntax. The query field accepts the same operators as the Gmail search bar, so you can narrow results further (for example, by sender or date). 
 Testing-mode token expiry. As noted in the previous post, an External app in Testing status has a limited refresh token lifetime. If authorization suddenly fails after about a week, register the authentication on the Desktop Agent again. 
 Wrapping Up 
 With these seven activities, a BPA automation can do nearly everything you'd do by hand in a Gmail inbox: find an email, read it and save its attachments, mark it as processed, send a new message, reply into a thread, and, when needed, delete one for good. They all run on the single setup from the previous post. 
 If you want to take this further into a complete invoice flow, you can combine the pieces from this series yourself. Each post covers one layer: the first builds the invoice approval process, the second sets up Document AI extraction on a trial instance, the third wires extraction into the approval process, and the fourth connects BPA to Google Workspace and fetches the attachments. This post adds the remaining Gmail activities on top of that setup. The fetched PDFs from the Gmail steps can serve as the source folder for the extraction automation in the second and third posts. 
 Each part is covered and tested on its own, and the connection points (a folder of PDFs, then extraction, then a call to the approval process) are the same ones those posts already use. If you would like the decision to go back to the sender as a reply in the original email thread, the Send Reply and Reply All activities are the ones to look at. The approval emails in the earlier posts are sent from the process itself, so that part would need some extra wiring.

title: SAP_TM - New condition for means of transport and vehicle type determination.
author: Rogerio_Lima1
text:
SAP_TM - New condition for means of transport and vehicle type determination. 
 Smarter Planning Starts with the Right Rules 
 In SAP Transportation Management (TM), knowing how goods move is just as important as knowing where they're going. The Means of Transport (MTr) and Equipment Type Determination feature empowers logistics planners to automate and standardize the selection of trucks, locomotives, and containers — all driven by configurable business rules. 
 This blog walks you through how to define the conditions that power this determination and how the system puts them to work across your planning processes. 
 What Is MTr/Equipment Type Determination? 
 At its core, this feature uses business rules to automatically determine: 
 The appropriate means of transport (e.g., truck, train) 
 The appropriate equipment type (truck type, locomotive type, or container type) 
 These determined values feed directly into various planning processes, making your transportation execution more consistent and efficient. 
 Step 1: Define Your Condition 
 The foundation of this feature is a condition of one of the following types: 
 /SCMTMS/MTR_ET_DET — Determine Means of Transport/Equipment Types 
 The conditions are built on a decision table framework. Several access definitions are available out of the box (all starting with /SCMTMS/MTR*), including: 
 Source Location 
 Destination Location 
 Transportation Mode 
 You can remove any access definitions you don't need, keeping your condition lean and focused. 
 Step 2: Build Your Decision Table 
 Inside the decision table, you define rules — each row representing one rule. For each rule, you specify: 
 Input values — based on your selected data access definitions (e.g., specific source/destination locations or transportation modes). If no input value is specified, all values are considered. 
 Output values — the means of transport and/or equipment types to be determined. Output values are mandatory . 
 Input values can be defined flexibly using: 
 Multiples include and exclude conditions 
 Operators or patterns (or both) 
 Quantities are automatically converted , so unit mismatches are handled for you. 
 Step 3: Validate Your Rules 
 Before going live, the system provides several consistency and validity checks , including: 
 Whether the means of transport and equipment type combination is valid 
 Whether the equipment type is relevant for planning 
 These checks help ensure your rules are logically sound before they influence real planning runs. 
 Prerequisites Before Going Live 
 Before the determination can work end-to-end, ensure the following are in place: 
 Equipment Types : The Restricted Use in Planning checkbox must be deselected for your equipment types. Configure this under: Customizing for Transportation Management → Master Data → Resources → General Settings → Define Equipment Groups and Equipment Types 
 Note: Only truck types , locomotive types , and container types are supported. 
 Freight Unit Type : Activate determination and reference your condition in your freight unit type. Configure under: Customizing Transportation Management → Planning → Freight Unit → Define Freight Unit Types This is required for determination during freight unit creation or modification . 
 Planning Profile : Activate determination and reference your condition in your planning profile. This is required for dynamic determination . 
 Important: You must start your planning session with this planning profile, or assign it to your business document type, for the setting to take effect. 
 How Determination Works at Runtime 
 The system considers the following input criteria to determine the appropriate means of transport and equipment type: 
 Source and destination location data 
 Service level (sales) 
 Payer and ship-to party 
 Determination is performed at each requested stage where no means of transport is defined yet. If no equipment type is defined, the system also attempts to find one compatible with the existing means of transport. If both are already defined, the determination is skipped. 
 The determined values are copied into the stage . 
 Two Determination Modes 
 Automatic Determination (at Freight Unit Level) 
 This mode triggers when a freight unit is created or an unplanned freight unit is changed . The determined values are saved in the following fields: 
 Preferred Means of Transport 
 Preferred Equipment Type 
 Preferred Equipment Group 
 These fields are visible in: 
 Freight unit stage list and hierarchy in the Transportation Cockpit 
 Combined freight unit/package unit stage list and hierarchy in the Transportation Cockpit 
 Stage view of the freight unit user interface 
 If multiple results are returned, the first result is used . 
 Key behaviors to know: 
 The Origin of Entry field tells you whether a value was manually entered, system-determined, or sourced from a default route. 
 Re-determination is triggered when relevant fields change (locations, product, weight, service level, or quantities). 
 Manual changes to means of transport, equipment type, and equipment group are protected from automatic re-determination . 
 When creating a freight order from a freight unit (or assigning a freight unit to an existing freight order), the system copies the means of transport, equipment type, and equipment group into the freight order — but only if no value exists yet. Existing values are never overwritten . Incompatibility issues trigger a warning message . 
 When assigning freight units to a container unit (or creating one from a freight unit stage), the system copies the container type of the first assigned freight unit into the container unit. 
 Dynamic Determination (On-the-Fly) 
 This mode runs just before a planning engine is called and serves as a fallback when: 
 A previous determination provided no result, or 
 The freight unit stage doesn't contain a means of transport or equipment type 
 Dynamic determination is skipped if: 
 The relevant fields already contain a value 
 You have manually changed one of them 
 The Means of Transport field in the freight unit stage hierarchy of the Transportation Cockpit already contains a value 
 Dynamic determination is supported in the following planning processes: 

 Planning Process 

 Lane, distance and duration determination 

 Transportation requirement routing and scheduling 

 Load consolidation 

 Vehicle scheduling and routing optimization 

 Generation of transportation proposals 
 Extensibility: Available BAdIs 
 For advanced scenarios, SAP TM provides three Business Add-Ins (BAdIs) to extend the determination logic: 

 BAdI 
 Purpose 

 BAdI: Adjustment of Means of Transport Determination 
 Change input data and results directly in the determination engine 

 BAdI: Adjustment of Means of Transport Determination Results 
 Change input data and results during planning operations (called from planning engines) 

 BAdI: Relevance Check for Means of Transport Determination 
 Check the relevance of freight units for means of transport determination 
 These BAdIs are available under: Customizing for Transportation Management → Business Add-Ins (BAdIs) for Transportation Management → Planning → Means of Transport Determination 
 Summary 
 The MTr and Equipment Type Determination feature in SAP TM brings rule-based intelligence to your transportation planning. By defining flexible conditions, building decision tables, and leveraging both automatic and dynamic determination modes, you can ensure the right equipment is always matched to the right shipment — automatically, consistently, and at scale.

 Thank you and regards. 
 Rogerio Lima.

title: SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model: Consuming Data Products from SAP BDC
author: Angelou
text:
SAP Profitability and Performance Management Cloud Universal Model (SAP PaPM Cloud UM) introduces the BDC Data Product connection type, enabling you to access SAP Business Data Cloud (SAP BDC) harmonized data products through a Targeted HANA Schema maintained within this connection. This allows you to use standardized, business-ready data directly in your modeling projects without custom integration work. 
 Before you dive in, take a moment to review the key terms used throughout this documentation. Understanding these will help you navigate the content more easily. See, Application Help for Universal Model – BDC Data Product 
 Prerequisites 
 You must have an SAP BDC Data Product installed in your SAP HANA Cloud or SAP Datasphere. 
 For more information, see Access and Query a Data Product in SAP HANA Cloud , Installing Marketplace Data Products - SAP Datasphere . 
 You must have the required roles for the creation of connection. See, Manage Connections . 
 You must have an Uploaded CSN Interop JSON or BDC API Resource ORD ID for fetching the metadata, allowing the application to locate and pull the correct blueprint of Data Products. 
 For more information, see Data Products . 
 Setting Up the BDC Data Product Connection 
 Setting up a BDC Data Product connection will feel familiar if you've worked with HANA Schema connections. It shares the same core fields: Connection ID, Description, and Tenant Specific Configuration, with the addition of Default Key 

 Importing the BDC Data Product Metadata 
 To complete the connection setup, import the metadata of the BDC Data Product you want to consume by uploading its CSN Interop JSON file. This file contains the data product structure including its entities, field names, data types, and relationships, and can be downloaded from the SAP API Business Hub - Data Products . 
 See the image below where you can download the CSN Interop JSON. Sample data product here: Data Product General Ledger Account 

 Once uploaded, pressing Import BDC Metadata will now load all available models from the CSN Interop JSON file, including their fields, relations, and other defined structures. From here, you can configure the models depending on your use case, selecting the specific fields, relations, and other components you need. 

 You can also rename the Target Function Name of each model to align with how you want to reference the Data Product table in your modeling. Please take note that these imported data products are generated as read-only Model HANA Functions, which can be activated and used for data access in your modeling projects. 

 The image above shows an example of a BDC Data Product model displaying its available fields and relations. All of these are based on the structure defined in the CSN Interop JSON file, which SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model automatically translates into a modeling UI that you can configure and use directly in your modeling. 
 Once you have configured your models by mapping the necessary fields and applying the required relations, you can proceed with Sync Model to synchronize the connection and Activate to make the data product available. After a successful activation, the BDC Data Product data is now ready to be consumed directly in your modeling projects within SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model. 
 Common Warnings and Errors 
 As you set up and configure your BDC Data Product connection, you may encounter some warnings and errors along the way. This section covers the most common ones to help you quickly identify and resolve them. 
 Warning: Schema Does Not Expose BDC Data Product Objects 

 This warning may appear during the creation of your BDC Data Product connection when the selected or synced model from the BDC Data Products is not detected in the Target HANA Schema. This typically means the Target HANA Schema does not have the corresponding BDC Data Product installed or is not accessible by the technical schema of SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model. 
 To resolve this, make sure the Target HANA Schema you have configured contains the BDC Data Products you intend to consume and is accessible to SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model. 
 Error: BDC Virtual Table or Consumption View Not Found 

 This error occurs during Activation when SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model searches for the synced or selected BDC Data Product from the created connection but cannot find it in the Target HANA Schema. During activation, Universal Model looks for the corresponding virtual table or consumption view of the BDC Data Product in the Target HANA Schema. When nothing is found, the activation fails with this error. 
 To resolve this, make sure the correct Target HANA Schema is maintained where the BDC Data Product is installed and visible to SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model. 
 All right, that will be it for now! With the BDC Data Product connection type now available in SAP PaPM Cloud Universal Model, consuming harmonized, business-ready data from SAP Business Data Cloud has never been more straightforward. By leveraging the CSN Interop JSON, you can quickly set up your connection, configure your models, and start using BDC Data Products directly in your calculations. See you again on my next blog post!

title: How Joule Assistants Orchestrate: From User Intent to Coordinated Actions
author: carlos_portillo
text:
Understanding how Joule Assistants orchestrate 
 I've had a lot of customer meetings lately where I'm asked to explain something I genuinely believe is one of the most impressive things SAP has built in AI: how Joule Assistants actually orchestrate work behind the scenes. With more meetings coming up and the same question certain to land again, I wasn't happy with the answer I'd been giving. I needed an easier way to explain it. 
 One night, I booked a restaurant for my wife and me. My wife has some dietary constraints due to allergies, so when the waiter arrived, she ordered the tasting menu but told him "no shellfish, no gluten, and no lactose." The waiter went to the kitchen, and while we were waiting, I found myself looking through the pass window. And something about the way the head chef was operating and directing the kitchen made me immediately see the analogy I'd been looking for. 
 In the kitchen, the head chef received our order, and I could see him reading and reasoning about it. He was understanding the request, breaking it down into tasks, and triggering, coordinating, and calling out tailored instructions to each station — accounting for every dietary constraint, adapting every course. "Course one, swap the crab for avocado, check the dressing is gluten-free, clean your board first." "Course three, seabass instead of scallop, olive oil only, no lactose on that pan." "Pastry — scrap the tart shell, do the berry sorbet, double-check it's gluten-free." 
 Each kitchen station got their specific instructions and nothing else. Some were working in parallel. Others were waiting for a prior step to complete. They didn't need to know what the other stations were doing. They just executed their piece and reported back. 
 Meanwhile, we were sitting at the table, having simply ordered dinner and waiting for it to arrive. What was happening in the kitchen was something we didn't need to think about. That's exactly how Joule Assistants work. 
 By the time dessert arrived, I had the whole thing mapped out. Let me walk you through it, because once you see the parallel, it's hard to unsee. 
 When a supply chain planner, a product engineer, or a maintenance supervisor type a request in Joule, that request moves through four distinct layers before anything happens in a SAP system. Each layer has a specific job, and each one maps neatly to someone in that restaurant. 
 Figure 1: The four layers between a user request and a system action 

 The first layer is the Joule Orchestrator . In the restaurant story, it would be the waiter. It reads your request, classifies the intent , checks the catalog of registered capabilities, enforces your access permissions, and routes to the best-matched Assistant. It doesn't cook anything. It just makes sure your order gets to the right kitchen and the right head chef. 
 The second layer is the Domain Assistant ; in our story, it would be the head chef. This is where the real orchestration happens. The Assistant doesn't follow a predefined script. It plans and reasons by leveraging an LLM, the same way a skilled manager would think through a complex problem. It reads the request, identifies what's actually being asked, figures out which specialists can help, decides the order of operations, dispatches them, evaluates what they return, and synthesizes everything into a recommendation. That's a lot of invisible work happening before you see a single result. 
 The third layer is the Domain Agents ; the kitchen stations. Each one is a specialist. They have a narrow, well-defined scope: one might be focused on demand trend analysis, another on inventory allocation modelling, a third on network capacity. They don't decide the broader workflow. They execute their piece, access the relevant SAP systems, and report back to the Assistant with structured findings. 
 The part that keeps coming back to me is the reasoning loop. Every request triggers a process inside the Domain Assistant. Understanding this is what separates a surface-level explanation from a real one. 
 Figure 2: The five-step reasoning loop every Domain Assistant runs 

 Step one is understanding the job. Not just reading the words, but working out the domain, the scope, the constraints, and what "done" actually looks like. 
 Step two is assembling the team. The Assistant selects which Agents to involve and deliberately excludes the ones that aren't relevant. 
 Step three is sequencing and dispatching tasks. If the tasks are independent of each other, the Assistant fans them out in parallel to save time. If they depend on each other — like a root cause analysis that must precede a resolution plan — they run in sequence, each one building on the last. 
 Step four is adaptive replanning. This is what separates orchestration from automation. Take a manufacturing quality use case example: the Manufacturing Assistant might initially plan to run an inspection readiness agent. But when the diagnostic agent comes back and reports that the root cause is contaminated supplier material — and not an equipment issue — the Assistant drops the inspection agent and adds a supplier nonconformance agent instead, mid-task. A rigid workflow would have run the wrong agents. The Assistant evaluated the evidence and changed course. 
 Step five is synthesis and governance. The Assistant combines all findings into a coherent recommendation and then decides about execution: sometimes the right answer is just showing you the insight, and sometimes it executes a direct action in a system. 
 Now we’re able to understand how a Joule Assistant orchestrates, but one piece is still missing: how do Assistants and Agents talk to each other? Every agent could be built by a different team, running on a different platform, in a different part of the enterprise. Without a shared protocol, connecting them would require building a custom bridge for every pair. This is exactly the problem the Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol was designed to solve. 
 Figure 3: The three phases of A2A communication between Assistants and Agents 

 The protocol works in three steps. The Assistant first discovers an Agent by reading its "digital business card" — a structured document that describes what the Agent can do, what inputs it expects, how to reach it, and what outputs it can deliver. Then it delegates by sending a formal task object that includes the intent, parameters, constraints, and a channel for real-time updates. Then the Agent executes and collaborates, streaming progress back as it works, not just returning a result at the end. 
 Alongside A2A, agents use MCP (Model Context Protocol) to connect to APIs, planning models, data products, knowledge graphs, and third-party services. If A2A is how agents talk to each other, MCP is how agents access the tools they need to do the work. 
 One additional thing to understand is that a Joule Assistant and a Joule Agent are built from the same technology. Both are developed in Joule Studio. Both use LLMs for planning and reasoning. Both run on SAP Business AI Platform. Both are registered in the SAP AI Agent Hub. Both use the A2A and MCP protocols. Technically, they are the same construct, however, what differentiates them is a design decision. An Assistant is built with a broad, role-aware scope and the authority to coordinate others. An Agent is built with a narrow, task-specific scope and the authority to execute within it. Same kitchen, but different job descriptions. 
 When a planner, engineer, or supervisor makes a request in Joule, they express their intent once. The Joule Orchestrator routes it. The Assistant reasons through it and delegates the tasks. The Agents execute. The systems get updated. The human gets a recommendation and approves the action. Users never needed to know which agents were involved, in what order, or which systems were touched. They simply got an answer.

Hello SAP Community, 
 I'm currently testing Planning Calendars in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and I would like to understand the expected standard behavior. 
 Business Requirement 
 The customer wants to generate planned orders according to specific planning frequencies: 
 Daily 
 Weekly (every Monday) 
 Every 2 weeks (Monday) 
 Every 3 weeks (Monday) 
 Monthly 
 To achieve this, we created several Planning Calendars: 
 CAL = Daily 
 HEB = Weekly (Monday) 
 J15 = Every 2 Weeks (Monday) 
 3SM = Every 3 Weeks (Monday) 
 MEN = Monthly 
 According to SAP documentation, Planning Calendars can be used together with a periodic lot-sizing procedure and can define flexible planning periods. 
 Configuration 
 Planning Calendar 
 Planning Calendars have been created and periods are generated correctly. 
 Lot-Sizing Procedure 
 A custom lot-sizing procedure was created: 
 Lot Sizing Type = P (Period Lot Size) 
 Lot Size Key = K (Periods According to Planning Calendar) 
 Number of Periods = 1 
 Material Master 
 MRP 1 
 MRP Type = PD 
 Lot Sizing Procedure = ZC 
 MRP 2 
 Planning Calendar = HEB 
 Expected Result 
 Since the Planning Calendar HEB defines weekly periods starting every Monday, we expected MRP to generate planned orders according to those Planning Calendar periods. 
 For example: 
 Monday → Sunday = Period 1 
 Monday → Sunday = Period 2 
 etc. 
 Actual Result 
 MRP generates planned orders successfully. 
 However: 
 Planned orders are not always generated on Monday. 
 Multiple planned orders may be generated on the same date. 
 The resulting dates do not seem to follow the Planning Calendar periods as expected. 
 Question 
 Has anyone implemented a similar requirement? 
 Specifically: 
 Is Lot Size Key K (Periods According to Planning Calendar) sufficient to make MRP generate planned orders according to Planning Calendar periods? 
 Are additional material master settings required? 
 Is the Planning Calendar only used for grouping requirements while planned order dates are calculated independently? 
 How do you achieve a planning cadence such as: 
 every Monday 
 every 2 weeks on Monday 
 every 3 weeks on Monday 
 in standard S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition? 
 Any feedback or examples would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thanks!

title: DIP_AD010007 and single-use restriction
author: SAPSupport
text:
We need to apply a customer-specific item sequence during Dynamic Item Processing (DIP) so that the resulting items are ordered as required for subsequent business processes. We intend to implement the necessary logic using BAdI DIP_AD010007. 
 However, the BAdI is defined without the “Multiple Use” flag, and an SAP standard implementation, 
 /CPD/PWSSE_BPM_RRB, already exists in our system. This prevents us from activating an additional customer implementation alongside the existing SAP implementation. 
 We have identified the classic customer exit EXIT_SAPLAD15_015, with customer include ZXAD1U06, as a potential alternative. However, our development strategy is to remain as closely aligned as possible with SAP’s Clean Core guidance and to use supported, upgrade-stable extension points. Before proceeding with this alternative, we would like SAP to clarify the recommended approach and whether this exit remains appropriate for the requirement in our system release. 
 The current restriction blocks our intended BAdI-based implementation. We need a supported way to introduce the required item sequence without interfering with the existing SAP standard functionality. 
 Could you please clarify the following? 

 Is the single-use restriction intentional when SAP standard implementation /CPD/PWSSE_BPM_RRB is present, and how should customers add their own processing logic in this situation? 

 Is there an SAP Note, correction, or alternative extension point that addresses this scenario? 

 If EXIT_SAPLAD15_015 is the recommended solution, is its use supported alongside the existing BAdI implementation, and are there any execution-order dependencies or restrictions we need to consider? 

 Which approach does SAP recommend for this requirement in terms of Clean Core alignment and long-term upgrade stability? 
 We would appreciate guidance on a supported implementation path that preserves the existing SAP functionality and allows us to meet the item-sorting requirement.

title: BPC ADSO in Planning Session shows request “completed with errors” in RSMNG – how to clear the error
author: shangfj621
text:
Hello SAP BW/4HANA experts, 
 I need help with a BPC-related ADSO where a request shows “completed with errors” in RSMNG, even though the data is present and the ADSO is working correctly in Planning Session. 
 Environment: 
 SAP BW/4HANA [version] 
 ADSO is a BPC model (planning-enabled ADSO) 
 RSOADSO-PLANNING_MODE = 'X' (correct for this ADSO) 
 Real-time behavior in RSMNG shows Planning Session – this is the intended state for this BPC model 
 Data is written via BPC planning, not via BW DTP or process chain 
 Relevant tables: RSPMPROCESS, RSPMREQUEST, RSPMLOG, RSPMTRACE 
 Problem description: 
 In RSMNG, there is a data request that shows “completed with errors” . 
 When I double-click the error, only the PROCESS_TSN is displayed — there is no actual error text. 

 In table RSPMPROCESS, there is a process with: 
 PROCESS_TYPE = 'PLAN' 
 PROCESS_STATUS = 'R' 
 This process was not triggered by a process chain, and the PLAN process is about three months old. 

 RSPMREQUEST contains record with PROCESS_STATUS = 'GG' and LAST_PROCESS_TSN WITH the error process tsn for this ADSO. 

 I have not deleted or modified this 'R' record yet. 
 In the log fields, the combined message appears as: 
 RSPMTRACE,100,0,2256,G,6 

 However, table RSPMTRACE is empty. 
 Data loads (BPC planning writes) still work, and subsequent process chain loads also complete normally. 
 My goal is: 
 Clear the “completed with errors” status in RSMNG 
 Make the data with error info can be activated. 
 Remove the inconsistent 'R' status so monitoring no longer shows an error 
 Questions: 
 What does the message RSPMTRACE,100,0,2256,G,6 mean? 
 Why is there a request showing “completed with errors” but no error details? 
 Is it safe to delete the old RSPMPROCESS PLAN record with status 'R'? Or should it be changed to 'G' instead? 
 Will deleting or changing this record affect the BPC planning data already written to the ADSO? 
 Is there a standard SAP note or repair program for this kind of RSPM status inconsistency in a BPC planning ADSO? 
 How can I make the request activatable without losing the already-written BPC planning data? 
 Has anyone seen this behavior where BPC planning data writes successfully but the RSPM PLAN process remains in status 'R' and RSMNG shows “completed with errors”? 
 Any guidance would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thanks.
